title: CFTR F508del carrier status (informational) · CFTR
summary: F508del is the most common cystic fibrosis (CF) variant. It makes up about 70% of CF alleles in people with European ancestry. About 1 in 25 to 30 people in that group carries one copy. This report checks only F508del. It is not carrier screening. Clinical screening tests many CFTR variants. If you are planning a family and want carrier information, ask a doctor or genetic counselor about proper testing.

interpretations.TCTTTCTT: No F508del deletion detected at this site. Important caveat: this checks only one CFTR variant out of the hundreds that can cause cystic fibrosis, so it does not rule out carrier status. Clinical carrier screening, which covers many CFTR variants, is the appropriate route for family-planning decisions; a genetic counselor can explain the options.
interpretations.TTCTT: One copy of F508del, which is consistent with CF carrier status. Carriers are healthy. If both partners carry a CF-causing variant, each pregnancy has a 1-in-4 chance of CF. Consumer arrays can misread this site. A clinical lab should confirm the result before you act on it. A genetic counselor can explain what it means for family planning.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of F508del. This is the most common genotype in people with CF, which is usually found in childhood. This result would be unexpected in an adult with no known CF. An array error is likely because this site is hard to read. A clinical lab should confirm the result. You should also speak with a genetic counselor.

title: FSH hormone levels · FSHB promoter (-211G>T)
summary: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) helps eggs mature and supports sperm production. rs10835638 lies in the FSHB promoter and lowers gene transcription. The T allele is linked to lower average blood FSH. In men, studies also link it to slightly smaller testes and lower sperm measures. Effects on fertility are small and differ across studies. A blood test measures FSH far better than genotype.

interpretations.GG: The common genotype, associated with typical FSHB promoter activity and average FSH levels at this locus. FSH levels still vary widely with age, cycle timing, and many other genetic and non-genetic factors.
interpretations.GT: One copy of the T allele, which reduces FSHB transcription in laboratory studies. Associated on average with somewhat lower circulating FSH. This is a small shift in hormone levels, not a fertility verdict; measured hormone levels are far more informative than genotype.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the lower-expression T allele, found in a few percent of people of European ancestry. Associated with the lowest average FSH levels of the three genotypes; in men, studies have linked this genotype to lower average FSH and modestly reduced sperm parameters. The association is preliminary and does not determine fertility for any individual.

title: Recurrent pregnancy loss · ANXA5 M2 haplotype
summary: Annexin A5 forms a protective anticoagulant shield on the placental surface. The M2 haplotype of the ANXA5 promoter, tagged here by rs112782763, reduces ANXA5 expression and has been associated with roughly 2x the odds of recurrent pregnancy loss in some case-control studies. The evidence base is small and results are mixed across populations, so this should be read as a preliminary association, not a prediction. Pregnancy loss is common and usually unrelated to this haplotype.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the M2-tagging allele at this position. This genotype is not associated with the reduced ANXA5 promoter activity linked to the M2 haplotype. Most pregnancy losses have causes unrelated to ANXA5, so this result says little either way about individual pregnancy outcomes.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele that tags the M2 haplotype, carried by roughly 10-15% of people of European ancestry. Some studies associate M2 carriage with about 1.5-2x the average odds of recurrent pregnancy loss; others find no effect. This is one small, preliminary factor among many, and most carriers have uncomplicated pregnancies. Anyone experiencing recurrent loss deserves a full clinical evaluation regardless of this result.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the uncommon T allele that tags M2. Some studies link this result to the lowest average ANXA5 promoter activity and slightly higher odds of repeat pregnancy loss. Data on this rare genotype are thin. This is one early finding among many factors. A clinician or genetic counselor can review it as part of a full evaluation.

citations.label: Bogdanova et al., Hum Mol Genet 2007

title: Age at natural menopause · MCM8
summary: MCM8 helps repair DNA in developing eggs. rs16991615 is one of the strongest single variants linked to menopause timing. Each A allele changes Glu341 to Lys. Each copy is linked to natural menopause about one year later and slightly higher anti-Mullerian hormone on average. People with the same genotype still differ by many years.

interpretations.GG: The most common genotype. Associated with average menopause timing at this locus. Smoking, ovarian surgery, family history, and many other genetic variants shift the actual age far more than any single variant.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A allele, carried by roughly 10-15% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with natural menopause about 0.9-1.1 years later than GG, and with slightly higher average anti-Mullerian hormone (a marker of ovarian reserve). A modest average shift, not a schedule.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the less common A allele. Associated on average with natural menopause roughly two years later than GG, the largest effect of any common single variant known for this trait. Even so, this is an average across populations; individual timing varies widely and depends on many other factors.

title: Dizygotic twinning · FSHB region
summary: Fraternal (dizygotic) twinning runs in families on the mother's side, partly through variants that raise follicle-stimulating hormone and make double ovulation more likely. Near the FSHB gene, the common rs11031006 G allele is associated with higher average FSH levels and roughly 1.2-1.3x the odds of being a mother of dizygotic twins per copy. This cross-references the FSHB promoter report: both loci act through FSH signaling. Identical twinning is unrelated to this variant.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the common G allele, which is the twinning-associated allele at this locus. Associated with modestly higher average FSH and, in mothers, roughly 1.2-1.3x the odds of a dizygotic twin pregnancy per G copy compared with carrying A alleles. Dizygotic twinning still depends heavily on maternal age, ancestry, and chance.
interpretations.AG: One copy of each allele. The A allele is associated with lower average FSH levels and somewhat lower odds of dizygotic twinning; this genotype sits in between the two homozygous groups on average. The absolute chance of a twin pregnancy remains low for all genotypes.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the less common A allele, which has about 8% frequency in European-ancestry groups. This result is linked to the lowest average FSH at this site and lower odds of a fraternal twin pregnancy. It matters only for the partner who makes eggs. Its effect is small next to age and family history.

citations.label: Mbarek et al., Am J Hum Genet 2016

title: Age at first period · LIN28B
summary: LIN28B helps control when development happens. Variation near it was among the first genetic links to puberty timing found by genome-wide studies. At rs7759938, each C allele is linked to a first period about 1 to 1.5 months later. It is also linked to later puberty milestones in both sexes. This shift is tiny next to the normal range of several years.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, carried by roughly 10-15% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with menarche about 2-3 months later than TT, and with slightly later puberty timing in boys as well. A shift of weeks against a backdrop of years of normal variation.
interpretations.CT: One copy of each allele, associated with intermediate average puberty timing: roughly 1-1.5 months later menarche than TT on average. Nutrition, body composition, and hundreds of other variants each contribute; this is one small factor.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of T, the most common genotype. This group has the earliest average puberty timing at this site. The gap from CC is only about two to three months. One variant says very little about when any one person will develop.

title: Endometriosis · WNT4 region (1p36)
summary: Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue like the uterine lining grows outside the uterus. It affects about 1 in 10 people with a uterus and is partly inherited. The 1p36 site near WNT4 is one of the most often replicated genetic links. WNT4 helps form the female reproductive tract. Each rs7521902 A allele is linked to about 1.2 times the average odds of endometriosis.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the A risk allele. Associated with somewhat lower average odds of endometriosis at this locus. This does not rule anything out: most endometriosis risk comes from other genetic and non-genetic factors, and symptoms such as severe pelvic pain warrant medical attention regardless of genotype.
interpretations.AC: One copy of A. This result is linked to about 1.2 times the average odds of endometriosis compared with CC. It is a small shift from one of many sites, not a prediction. Only a clinical evaluation can establish the condition.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, carried by roughly 7-8% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with about 1.4-1.5x the odds of endometriosis relative to CC. Still one small factor among many: most people with this genotype never develop endometriosis, and most cases occur in people without it.

title: Polycystic ovary syndrome · DENND1A
summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormone condition that can involve irregular ovulation and high androgen levels. DENND1A at 9q33.3 emerged from the first genome-wide PCOS studies in Han Chinese groups. Each rs2479106 G allele was linked to about 1.3 times the odds of PCOS. Studies of this variant in European-ancestry groups have had mixed results. The evidence is preliminary.

interpretations.AA: No copies of the G allele that was associated with PCOS in the discovery studies. Associated with average or somewhat lower odds at this locus. PCOS risk involves many genes plus weight, insulin signaling, and other factors, so this result carries little individual weight.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the G allele. In Han Chinese cohorts this was associated on average with roughly 1.3x the odds of PCOS; studies in European-ancestry populations have not consistently reproduced the finding. A preliminary, ancestry-dependent association and one small factor among many.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, a common genotype worldwide. Associated in the discovery cohorts with the highest average odds at this locus (roughly 1.6-1.8x versus AA), but the inconsistent replication outside East Asian cohorts means this should be read cautiously. PCOS can only be established through clinical evaluation of symptoms and hormone levels.

title: FSH receptor sensitivity · FSHR Asn680Ser
summary: FSH receptors on ovarian cells control how strongly the ovary responds to FSH. rs6166 changes amino acid 680 from asparagine to serine. Ser/Ser carriers have slightly higher average FSH at baseline. Early IVF studies found that they needed more stimulation medicine on average for the same response. Both forms are common and work with normal fertility. This result concerns average IVF response, not the ability to conceive.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, encoding Ser680/Ser680. Associated with a slightly less sensitive FSH receptor: modestly higher average basal FSH, and in IVF studies a higher average requirement for FSH stimulation to reach the same response. Roughly a quarter of people carry this genotype, and it is fully compatible with normal fertility.
interpretations.CT: One copy of each allele (Asn680/Ser680), the most common genotype in most populations. Associated with intermediate average receptor sensitivity and basal FSH between the two homozygous groups. Any practical relevance is limited to fertility-treatment settings, where clinicians rely on measured hormone levels rather than genotype.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, encoding Asn680/Asn680. Associated with a somewhat more sensitive FSH receptor: lower average basal FSH and, on average, a stronger ovarian response to a given stimulation dose in IVF studies. These are average shifts in dose-response, not a measure of fertility.

citations.label: Perez Mayorga et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2000

title: Pregnancy and clotting · Factor V Leiden
summary: Factor V Leiden (rs6025, Arg506Gln) is the most common inherited variant that raises clot risk. About 3% to 5% of people with European ancestry carry it. Pregnancy also raises clot risk. Carriers have higher average odds of a vein clot during pregnancy and after birth. Studies also link the variant to about 1.5 to 2 times the odds of pregnancy loss. Most carriers have pregnancies without these problems. This report is for information only. If you carry the variant and plan a pregnancy, consider speaking with a clinician or genetic counselor.

interpretations.CC: No Factor V Leiden variant detected. Clotting tendency at this locus is typical. Other inherited and acquired factors can still affect clotting risk in pregnancy, and this single-variant result is not a full thrombophilia work-up.
interpretations.CT: One copy of Factor V Leiden. About 3% to 5% of people with European ancestry have this result. It is linked to several times the average odds of a vein clot. Pregnancy and medicines that contain estrogen raise that risk further. Studies also link it to about 1.5 to 2 times the odds of pregnancy loss. Most carriers never have a clot, and most pregnancies have no related problem. A clinical lab should confirm the result. A clinician or genetic counselor can put it in context.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of Factor V Leiden. This is rare, affecting about 1 in 1,000 to 2,500 people with European ancestry. It is linked to much higher average odds of a vein clot than one copy. Pregnancy raises that risk further. A clinical lab should confirm this result. Speak with a clinician or genetic counselor, especially before pregnancy. The result shifts probability; it does not make any outcome certain.
